subject: english-literature
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: How does Iago manipulate Cassio into losing his position?
options: By forging a letter of treason
By getting Cassio drunk so he brawls and is dismissed
questions.explain: Iago plies Cassio with drink, provoking a fight that leads Othello to strip Cassio of his rank.

questions.q: The tragic structure of a Shakespearean play is often described as following a five-act movement; the 'climax' typically marks:
options: the turning point after which the hero's fortunes decisively decline
questions.explain: In the five-act model the climax is the pivot from which the hero's fortunes irreversibly fall toward catastrophe.

questions.q: What object becomes the central 'proof' Iago uses to convince Othello of Desdemona's infidelity?
questions.explain: The handkerchief Othello gave Desdemona, planted in Cassio's lodging, becomes the false 'ocular proof'.

questions.q: How does Othello describe himself in his final speech?
options: 'A man more sinned against than sinning'
'One that loved not wisely, but too well'
questions.explain: Othello asks to be remembered as one who 'loved not wisely, but too well' before killing himself.

questions.q: Complete Othello's line: 'O, beware, my lord, of jealousy; / It is the ___ monster which doth mock / The meat it feeds on.'
questions.explain: Iago, ironically, warns Othello of the 'green-eyed monster' he himself is feeding.

questions.q: In Doctor Faustus, the overreaching protagonist who barters his soul for forbidden knowledge illustrates the tragic convention of:
options: aspiration and transgression punished by an inexorable downfall
the restoration of order through marriage
questions.explain: Faustus embodies tragic overreaching, his transgressive ambition driving an inescapable damnation.

questions.q: Iago's line 'I am not what I am' encapsulates which idea?
options: His duplicity and the gap between his mask and his true self
questions.explain: 'I am not what I am' announces Iago's fundamental deceit and self-concealment.

questions.q: Aristotle valued a 'complex' plot over a 'simple' one because the complex plot includes:
options: both peripeteia and anagnorisis, producing a stronger tragic effect
questions.explain: For Aristotle the finest tragic plots combine reversal and recognition, intensifying pity and fear.

questions.q: How does Othello come to marry Desdemona?
options: Through a betrothal organised by Iago
By winning her in a contest set by the Duke
By eloping secretly, which Brabantio condemns to the Senate
Through an arranged marriage by her father Brabantio
questions.explain: Othello and Desdemona marry secretly, and Brabantio accuses Othello of bewitching her before the Senate.

questions.q: How does the play treat the theme of race?
options: Othello as 'the Moor' is othered, and racist slurs mark his outsider status
Race is praised as irrelevant by all characters
Othello is mocked only for his age
questions.explain: Othello is repeatedly racialised as 'the Moor', and Iago and Brabantio deploy racist language to isolate him.

questions.q: Which theme is most central to Othello?
options: Sexual jealousy and its destructive power
questions.explain: Jealousy, the 'green-eyed monster', drives Othello to destroy what he loves.

questions.q: What role does Roderigo play in Iago's schemes?
options: He is Iago's trusting dupe, funding the plot to win Desdemona
questions.explain: Roderigo, in love with Desdemona, is exploited and bankrolled by Iago, who finally kills him.

questions.q: A key debate in tragedy concerns whether the hero's fall is driven by 'fate' or 'free will'; this matters because:
options: it shapes how far we hold the hero responsible and how we read the play's moral vision
it decides the number of acts
it determines the metre of the verse
questions.explain: The balance of fate and choice governs the audience's apportioning of blame and the tragedy's view of human agency.

questions.q: What was the contemporary Jacobean attitude that the play partly engages with regarding 'the Moor'?
options: There was anxiety and prejudice toward Moors as exotic outsiders
Moors were the ruling class of England
Moors were forbidden from the stage
questions.explain: Early modern English audiences viewed Moors with suspicion and exoticism, a context the play exploits.

questions.q: Othello was probably first performed around which period?
questions.explain: Othello dates to roughly 1603-04, early in the reign of James I.

questions.q: The function of the 'chorus' in Greek tragedy was most often to:
options: play the role of the tragic hero
stage the violent deeds on stage
comment on the action, voice communal response and offer moral or thematic reflection
questions.explain: The chorus mediates between stage and audience, commenting on events and articulating the wider moral perspective.

questions.q: How does Desdemona die at the end of the play?
options: Othello smothers her in their bed
questions.explain: Othello smothers Desdemona in her bed, convinced of her adultery.

questions.q: What does Othello demand of Iago, in a line revealing his shift toward needing evidence?
options: 'I'll have some proof... the ocular proof'
questions.explain: Othello's demand for 'ocular proof' shows his fatal need for visible certainty Iago exploits.

questions.q: Critics often describe Iago's lack of a sufficient motive using which phrase?
questions.explain: Coleridge's phrase 'motiveless malignity' captures how Iago's stated motives never fully explain his evil.

questions.q: Which description best fits Iago's character?
options: A scheming villain who deceives everyone around him
questions.explain: Iago is the play's manipulative antagonist who engineers Othello's downfall while feigning honesty.

questions.q: In Aristotle's Poetics, 'hamartia' is best understood as:
options: the audience's emotional purging at the play's close
the tragic hero's error of judgement or flaw that precipitates their downfall
the reversal of fortune from good to bad
questions.explain: Hamartia is the tragic hero's mistake or flaw, the error from which the catastrophe ultimately flows.

questions.q: At the start of Othello, why is Iago resentful of Othello?
options: Othello has promoted Cassio to lieutenant over Iago
Othello refuses to fight the Turks
Othello has insulted Iago's wife Emilia
questions.explain: Iago opens the play complaining that Othello chose Cassio as lieutenant, passing him over.

questions.q: What is notable about Cassio's attitude toward Desdemona?
options: He is courteous and respectful, which Iago twists into evidence
He secretly loves her and plots with her
questions.explain: Cassio's genuine courtesy toward Desdemona is manipulated by Iago to suggest an affair.

questions.q: 'Catharsis', in Aristotelian tragedy, denotes:
options: the chorus's commentary on the action
the purging or cleansing of pity and fear in the audience
the hero's sudden recognition of the truth
questions.explain: Catharsis is the purgation of the emotions of pity and fear that tragedy arouses and then releases in the audience.

questions.q: A.C. Bradley's influential approach to Shakespearean tragedy is associated with close attention to:
options: the psychology and 'character' of the tragic hero
the printing history of the quartos
questions.explain: Bradley's criticism foregrounds the tragic hero's character and inner psychology as the engine of the tragedy.

questions.q: Shakespearean tragedy typically departs from strict classical models by:
options: mingling subplots, comic elements and a broad sweep of time and place
questions.explain: Shakespeare loosens the classical unities, weaving subplots, comedy and expansive action into the tragic structure.

questions.q: What happens to Emilia in the final scene?
options: She takes her own life beside Desdemona
Iago kills her after she exposes his lies
questions.explain: Emilia reveals the truth about the handkerchief and Iago stabs her to silence her.

questions.q: The convention of the 'tragic waste' refers to:
options: the destruction of much that is valuable, leaving a sense of loss beyond the hero alone
questions.explain: Tragic waste names the loss of admirable lives and potential, deepening the catastrophe's emotional weight.

questions.q: In tragedy, 'hubris' refers to:
options: the hero's humility before the gods
excessive pride or overreaching that affronts the moral or divine order
questions.explain: Hubris is overweening pride or presumption that violates limits and invites the hero's downfall.

questions.q: How does Othello die?
options: He is executed by the Venetian state
He takes his own life with a hidden weapon
questions.explain: Othello stabs himself after recognising his terrible error, dying beside Desdemona.
